structures.name: tongue
structures.definition: Muscular organ filling the floor of the mouth, covered with taste buds.
structures.function: Moves food for chewing, forms the bolus, starts swallowing and shapes speech.
structures.why: Muscle fibres running in three directions let it change shape freely.

notes.dentistry: Examine all its surfaces, including the sides and underside, for ulcers or white or red patches.
notes.nursing: A dry, coated tongue suggests dehydration or poor oral care.

structures.name: salivary glands
structures.definition: Glands under the jaw and under the tongue that drain into the mouth.
structures.function: Produce saliva, which moistens food, starts starch digestion and protects the teeth.
structures.why: Saliva lubricates swallowing and buffers acid that would dissolve enamel.

notes.dentistry: Reduced saliva (dry mouth from medication or radiotherapy) sharply raises caries risk.
notes.medicine: Stones most often form in the submandibular gland because its saliva is thick and its duct runs uphill.

structures.name: oesophagus
structures.definition: Muscular tube about 25 cm long running from the pharynx through the chest behind the trachea to the stomach.
structures.function: Moves swallowed food to the stomach by waves of contraction (peristalsis).
structures.why: Its lower sphincter stops stomach acid flowing back up.

notes.nursing: Confirm nasogastric tube position before use; a misplaced tube may be in the airway instead.
notes.medicine: Narrows at three points: the cricopharyngeus, where the aortic arch and left bronchus cross it, and the diaphragm.

structures.name: stomach
structures.definition: J-shaped muscular bag in the upper left abdomen, below the diaphragm.
structures.function: Stores food, churns it with acid and enzymes, and releases it slowly into the duodenum.
structures.why: Storage lets us eat meals rather than graze, and acid kills many swallowed microbes.

notes.nursing: Gastric aspirate pH of 5.5 or below helps confirm nasogastric tube position.
notes.medicine: Peptic ulcers are most often caused by H. pylori or NSAIDs.

structures.name: duodenum
structures.definition: C-shaped first part of the small intestine, curving around the head of the pancreas.
structures.function: Receives bile and pancreatic juice and begins most chemical digestion.
structures.why: Mixing acid food with alkaline juices here neutralises it and activates enzymes.

notes.medicine: Duodenal ulcers are commoner than gastric ulcers; pain often eases with food.

structures.name: jejunum
structures.definition: Middle part of the small intestine, mostly in the upper left abdomen.
structures.function: Absorbs most nutrients from digested food.
structures.why: Tall folds and villi give it a huge surface area for absorption.

notes.medicine: Feeding tubes (jejunostomies) are placed here when the stomach cannot be used.

structures.name: ileum
structures.definition: Final and longest part of the small intestine, ending at the caecum.
structures.function: Absorbs vitamin B12 and bile salts and the remaining nutrients.
structures.why: Recycling bile salts here saves the liver making new ones.

notes.medicine: Crohn’s disease most often affects its last part; removal can cause B12 deficiency.

structures.name: appendix
structures.definition: Narrow finger-like tube hanging from the caecum in the lower right abdomen.
structures.function: Contains lymphoid tissue and may store helpful gut bacteria.
structures.why: It may act as a reserve of gut bacteria after diarrhoeal illness.

notes.nursing: Pain moving from around the navel to the lower right abdomen suggests appendicitis; keep nil by mouth and escalate.
notes.medicine: McBurney’s point lies one third of the way from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus.

structures.name: ascending colon
structures.definition: Part of the large intestine rising up the right side of the abdomen from the caecum to the liver.
structures.function: Absorbs water and salts from the liquid contents arriving from the small intestine.
structures.why: It begins turning liquid waste into firm stool.

notes.medicine: Right-sided bowel cancers often present with anaemia rather than a change in bowel habit.

structures.name: transverse colon
structures.definition: Part of the large intestine crossing the abdomen from right to left, hanging below the stomach.
structures.function: Continues absorbing water and moving stool toward the left side.
structures.why: Hanging on its own mesentery lets it move and stretch as it fills.

notes.medicine: Its middle hangs low and can reach the pelvis in thin people.

structures.name: descending colon
structures.definition: Part of the large intestine running down the left side of the abdomen.
structures.function: Stores and moves formed stool toward the rectum.
structures.why: Fixed to the back wall, it is a steady channel for stool.

notes.medicine: Diverticula are common in the left colon in older adults.

structures.name: rectum
structures.definition: Final straight part of the large intestine in the pelvis, ending at the anal canal.
structures.function: Stores stool until it can be passed and triggers the urge to defecate.
structures.why: Stretch receptors in its wall signal when it is full.

notes.nursing: Rectal medications and enemas are given with the patient lying on the left side, following the bowel’s curve.

structures.name: liver
structures.definition: The largest internal organ, in the upper right abdomen under the diaphragm.
structures.function: Processes nutrients, makes bile and plasma proteins, stores glycogen and clears drugs and toxins.
structures.why: All blood from the gut passes through it first, so it can process what is absorbed.

notes.nursing: Jaundice, confusion and bruising suggest liver failure; check drug doses, as many are cleared here.
notes.medicine: Divided into eight functional segments by its blood supply (Couinaud).

structures.name: gallbladder
structures.function: Stores and concentrates bile and squeezes it into the duodenum after fatty meals.
structures.why: Releasing bile on demand delivers it when fat needs digesting.

notes.nursing: Pain under the right ribs after a fatty meal suggests gallstones.
notes.medicine: Murphy’s sign: pain stops a breath in when pressing below the right ribs.

structures.name: bile ducts
structures.definition: Branching tubes draining bile from the liver and the bile sac into the duodenum.
structures.function: Carry bile to the intestine to digest fat.
structures.why: They connect bile made in the liver with the gut where it is needed.

notes.medicine: A stone blocking the common bile duct causes jaundice; with fever and pain, think cholangitis.

structures.name: pancreas
structures.definition: Long gland lying behind the stomach, its head in the curve of the duodenum.
structures.function: Makes digestive enzymes and the hormones insulin and glucagon.
structures.why: It is both a digestive gland and an endocrine organ controlling blood sugar.

notes.nursing: Acute pancreatitis causes severe upper abdominal pain radiating to the back; monitor fluid balance closely.
notes.medicine: Gallstones and alcohol are the commonest causes of acute pancreatitis.

structures.name: spleen
structures.definition: Fist-sized organ in the upper left abdomen behind the stomach, under ribs 9–11.
structures.function: Filters old red cells and bacteria from the blood and helps mount immune responses.
structures.why: Blood flowing slowly through it lets white cells catch bacteria and old cells.

notes.sports: Avoid contact sport for several weeks after glandular fever: an enlarged spleen can rupture.
notes.medicine: After splenectomy, patients need vaccines and sometimes lifelong antibiotics.
